content: Uterine fibroids, also referred to as leiomyomas, are the most common benign tumors affecting the female pelvis. While some women with fibroids remain asymptomatic, others experience significant symptoms such as abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pain, or urinary complaints. Medical management options for fibroids are limited, and gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues are among the most effective pharmacological treatments. However, prolonged use of GnRH analogues is often restricted due to their adverse effects, including bone density loss and vasomotor symptoms. To mitigate these side effects, a strategy called add-back therapy involves the concurrent administration of additional medications during GnRH analogue treatment. Despite its potential benefits, there are concerns that add-back therapy may reduce the efficacy of GnRH analogues and may not fully prevent their adverse effects. The objective of this review was to evaluate the short-term (up to 12 months) effectiveness and safety of add-back therapy in women treated with GnRH analogues for fibroids associated with excessive uterine bleeding, pelvic pain, or urinary symptoms. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing GnRH analogues with and without add-back therapy. Fourteen RCTs were included, with data extracted from 12 studies involving 622 women. The primary outcome assessed was quality of life (QoL), along with secondary outcomes such as bone density, uterine volume, uterine bleeding, and vasomotor symptoms. 1. Medroxyprogesterone Acetate (MPA): No studies reported on QoL or uterine bleeding outcomes. There was no significant effect on bone mass (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.38, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.62 to 1.38, low-quality evidence). MPA was associated with an increase in uterine volume (mean difference [MD] 342.19 cm³, 95% CI 77.58 to 606.80, low-quality evidence). 2. Tibolone: Tibolone was associated with improved QoL, but the effect size was imprecise and could range from clinically insignificant to large (SMD 0.47, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.85, low-quality evidence). It reduced bone mass loss, with the effect size ranging from small to moderate (SMD 0.36, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.70, moderate-quality evidence). Tibolone was linked to an increase in uterine volume (MD 23.89 cm³, 95% CI 8.13 to 39.66, moderate-quality evidence). There was inconsistent evidence regarding uterine bleeding, with some studies reporting increased bleeding and others reporting no bleeding. Tibolone showed a significant benefit in reducing vasomotor symptoms in four studies, though the results were not pooled due to heterogeneity. 3. Raloxifene: There was no evidence of an effect on QoL (SMD 0.11, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.34, low-quality evidence). Raloxifene had a beneficial effect on bone mass (SMD 1.01, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.45, low-quality evidence). There was no clear evidence of an effect on uterine volume (MD 27.1 cm³, 95% CI -17.94 to 72.14, low-quality evidence), uterine bleeding, or vasomotor symptoms. 4. Estriol: No studies reported on QoL, uterine size, uterine bleeding, or vasomotor symptoms. Estriol was associated with reduced bone mass loss in one study (SMD 3.93, 95% CI 1.70 to 6.16, low-quality evidence). 5. Ipriflavone: No studies reported on QoL, uterine size, or uterine bleeding. Ipriflavone reduced bone mass loss in one study (SMD 2.71, 95% CI 2.14 to 3.27, low-quality evidence). There was no significant effect on vasomotor symptoms (relative risk [RR] 0.67, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.02, low-quality evidence). 6. Conjugated Estrogens: No studies reported on QoL, uterine size, uterine bleeding, or vasomotor symptoms. One study suggested that conjugated estrogens combined with GnRH analogues resulted in a greater reduction in uterine volume compared to placebo (MD 105.2 cm³, 95% CI 27.65 to 182.75, very low-quality evidence). The majority of studies included in this review had a high risk of bias, particularly due to lack of blinding. Additionally, all studies had a maximum follow-up duration of six months, which is insufficient to assess long-term outcomes such as fracture risk related to bone health. Conclusions: There is low to moderate quality evidence suggesting that tibolone, raloxifene, estriol, and ipriflavone may help preserve bone density during GnRH analogue treatment. Tibolone and MPA may also alleviate vasomotor symptoms. However, some add-back therapies, including MPA, tibolone, and conjugated estrogens, were associated with an increase in uterine volume. For other outcomes, such as QoL, uterine bleeding, and vasomotor symptoms, the evidence was either inconclusive or not reported. Further high-quality, long-term studies are needed to better understand the risks and benefits of add-back therapy in this context.
